primitives.name: Topological Ordering Optimization
primitives.verbatim_quote: Learn the ordering via sparse relaxations over the permutahedron (sparse operators: sparsemax/sparseMAP-style; connects to Gumbel-Sinkhorn approximations over the Birkhoff polytope).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'π': 'permutation vector in R^d, elements ordered by topological precedence', 'θ': 'sparse distribution over permutations, dimension d!', 'B': 'binary incidence matrix encoding valid DAG edges'}
primitives.assumptions: Observational data; Gaussian equal-variance error model; DAG ground truth; standardized variables.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When permutation space becomes intractable due to high-dimensional node sets (>10 nodes).

layer2.mapping: The permutahedron is isomorphic to the set of all topological orderings of a DAG, allowing continuous relaxation of discrete combinatorial optimization.
layer2.telemetry: Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) between estimated and true orderings.

primitives.name: Joint Edge Estimation
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Structure parameters θ learn a sparse distribution over orderings; edge parameters Φ (functional parameters per node f_j^{φ_j}) learned jointly end-to-end or alternately, or conditionally via any black-box subroutine (differentiability not required).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'Φ': 'set of functional parameters per node, f_j^{φ_j}', 'f_j': 'node-specific causal function mapping parent values to child value', 'φ_j': "vector of coefficients or weights for node j's functional form"}
primitives.assumptions: Any differentiable or non-differentiable edge estimator may be used; functional forms are flexible.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When edge estimation fails due to non-identifiability or high noise in observational data.

layer2.mapping: Edge functions derived from conditional dependencies given fixed ordering, enabling modular integration with arbitrary estimators.
layer2.telemetry: Structural Intervention Distance (SID) measuring causal path preservation.

primitives.name: Exact DAG Validity
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Three claimed advantages: (1) validity — optimizes over exact DAGs, not approximate ones; (2) modularity — any edge-optimization procedure, structural parameterization, loss; (3) end-to-end — alternate or joint optimization of ordering and edges.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'G': 'DAG with adjacency matrix A ∈ {0,1}^{d×d}', 'A_{ij}': 'edge from i to j exists iff 1, else 0', 'O': 'topological ordering vector π such that O_i < O_j implies i precedes j in DAG'}
primitives.assumptions: Graph must remain acyclic throughout optimization; edges only allowed from lower to higher indices in ordering.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure occurs when constraints on edge directionality are violated during iterative updates.

layer2.mapping: Each valid DAG corresponds uniquely to a permutation in the permutahedron, ensuring exactness of learned structures.
layer2.telemetry: Number of cycles detected in final graph (should be zero).

reasoning_traces.think:
The core innovation lies in decomposing DAG learning into two components: (1) topological ordering over the permutahedron—a convex polytope whose vertices correspond to valid topological orderings—and (2) edge estimation conditioned on this ordering. This separation allows for modular design where any edge estimator can be plugged in without compromising DAG validity. The permutahedron enables continuous relaxation using sparse operators like sparsemax, which approximate discrete permutations while maintaining differentiability for gradient descent. Theoretical guarantees include global sensitivity bounds relating SHD between orderings to Hamming-type disagreements. In practice, this framework supports both joint and alternating optimization strategies, offering flexibility in training dynamics. The key insight is that optimizing over permutations directly ensures that all intermediate graphs remain valid DAGs, unlike NOTEARS-style methods which optimize over approximate matrices. This dual advantage—validity and modularity—enables seamless integration with complex, non-differentiable edge estimators such as gradient boosting models within GSE’s architecture.
